paper_title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI agents working on long tasks often stop too soon and commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, behavior often called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. At every turn, the agent decides whether to take further step or to commit to an answer. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer. It does not show which turns helped, and it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator knows the rules linking the hidden answer to the evidence, so it can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which takes this posterior as the belief supported by the evidence. RLVB rewards the agent for taking further steps while this belief still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward depends only on the evidence the agent has gathered and needs no judge, critic or reward model. It never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action, although the update trains this line together with the action. We also introduce Pro-Worlds, benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views large world through small window and must decide when it has enough visual evidence to commit. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average and by 10.4% with expectation maximization (EM) as the learner. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. To find where this gain comes from, we group the answers by the evidence the agent has when it answers. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. For every method, 66 to 92% of the answers given with sufficient evidence are correct. The accuracy gain of the trained agent therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence, while at the same level of evidence its answers are no more accurate than those of the base model. The belief line shows how the trained agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model with the same line. Over all turns, its line is not consistently more exact than that of the base model, and each of its steps adds about as much evidence as step of the base model. Because the trained agent acts on its belief, we expect better reading of the evidence to translate into better answers. Date: November 25, 2026 Code: https://github.com/declare-lab/RLVB

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Agents that work over long horizons are now used in games, embodied settings, and other interactive environments (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a,b). Such an agent must keep working until it has gathered sufficient evidence to act (Bajcsy, 1988; Das et al., 2018). However, current agents often stop too early (Laban et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Cuadron et al., 2025) and answer with guess. This behavior is called laziness (Ma and Liu, 2025). In the cups task in figure 1, the agent lifts one cup at time to find hidden object. After two lifts, the evidence is not yet sufficient because the object could still be under either of two cups. The next action should therefore lift another cup instead of guessing. In our experiments, the base models often guess even after they write that several cups remain possible. 3 4 1 2 The agent must find the red cylinder. Cup 1 hides green cylinder and cup 3 is empty. The reported RLVB is trained with the action term. At every turn, an evidence-seeking agent should keep belief that matches the evidence. It should take steps aimed at what this belief leaves open. It should commit only when the belief identifies the answer. Knowing how much one knows and acting on it is called metacognition (Flavell, 1979). Metacognition has two parts: monitoring what one knows and controlling what one does with it (Nelson and Narens, 1990). Language models can often recognize what they know (Kadavath et al., 2022). However, the base models in our evaluations commit too early, even though our prompts tell them to commit only once the evidence identifies the answer. When they write belief line before each action, they commit at 3 to 68% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and this belief line still names several answers. They often state that the answer remains open and commit anyway. These models do not act on what their own belief line states. check in the harness that rejects the first answer does not solve this problem, because the harness cannot read the observations, as section 4.6 shows. Whether the evidence determines the answer depends on what the agent has observed. Only the agent reads these observations. The agents own belief can therefore guide each decision once the agent learns to act on it. We call an agent reliable when its answers are both correct and backed by sufficient evidence, because user who receives an answer usually cannot check how the agent reached it. Training an agent to make this decision reliably over long horizon is central problem in agentic reinforcement learning (RL). 2 RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is common way to train large language models on math (Shao et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025) and code (Le et al., 2022; Gehring et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025) tasks. verifier checks the final answer and rewards the model when the answer is correct (Lambert et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Kimi Team, 2025). Recent work trains multi-turn agents with the same kind of framework (Zhou et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b,a; Feng et al., 2025). Over long horizon, however, reward on the final answer cannot tell which steps helped and which steps caused failure (Minsky, 1961; Sutton and Barto, 2018). lucky guess is reinforced as fully as an answer supported by the evidence. careful search is penalized whenever the episode is lost. Agents also tend to answer before the evidence supports the final answer (Laban et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) or fall back on fixed patterns that ignore the evidence (Wang et al., 2025b, 2026b). As table 2 shows, the base models on HiddenGames give 64 to 97% of their answers before their evidence is sufficient, whether or not they write belief line. RL with the outcome reward even lowers the accuracy of these models on average. To credit single steps, recent work returns to the PPO framework (Schulman et al., 2017) and rewards every step with process reward (Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2024). This reward is often given by process reward model or an LLM judge (Cui et al., 2026; Khalifa et al., 2026). Yet the value of step is hard to estimate, because the critic of PPO is fitted to outcomes that depend on the hidden target. As figure 2(b) shows, an LLM judge that sees the target may reward lucky guess and penalize correct but still uncertain belief. The critic and the judge also make training more expensive, because the critic is second model trained next to the policy and the judge is called at every step. Agentic RL usually trains in sandbox simulator (Wang et al., 2025b,a; Feng et al., 2025). This simulator knows much more than whether the final answer is correct. It knows the hidden target and what each action will reveal about it. Prior work passes this privileged information to teacher or critic (Pinto et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019; Choudhury and Sodhi, 2025). In tasks where the agent gathers evidence, this information lets the simulator compute the exact posterior over the hidden answer after every step. This posterior is the belief state (Åström, 1965; Kaelbling et al., 1998). The final answer is then no longer the only thing the simulator can verify. The posterior is the belief supported by the evidence. The simulator can verify it at every step, just as RLVR verifies the answer at the end. This belief shows whether the agent should take further steps or answer. This moves us from reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB). At each turn, we give every method its full history of actions and observations. As result, no method has to remember what it has explored. From the exact posterior, the agent learns when to commit and when to keep working. The reward also scores which step the agent chooses next, but the trained agent does not choose more informative steps than the base model, as section 4.6 shows. Before each action, the agent states the answers it still sees as possible, such as Possible: cups 2, 4. This belief line shows whether the agent thinks it has sufficient evidence. The reward never reads this line. Because the update raises the likelihood of the whole turn, it still trains the line along with the action. As section 4.6 shows, the trained agent then learns to act on the line. The turns reward compares the agents next action to the action teacher chooses by looking ahead on the exact posterior (Howard, 1966). The reward can also score the stated belief against the posterior, but scoring the action is enough, as section 4.4 shows. The reward never pays for guess. It depends on the evidence the agent has gathered. It does not depend on which answer happens to be correct in the episode. In figure 1, cups 2 and 4 are still possible. Lifting another cup gets reward close to zero. Answering cup 4 gets about 7, whether or not the object is under cup 4. At each history, the agent samples several of its own turns and makes the higher-reward turns more likely. The learner uses either policy gradient that compares turns within group, as in GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), or expectation maximization (EM) (Dempster et al., 1977). RLVB needs no judge, critic or reward model because the posterior is exact. Our contributions are: RLVB. We use the simulators privileged information to compute the exact posterior after every step. We turn this posterior into process reward. This reward scores each action against teacher acting on the exact posterior. The reward never reads the agents belief line, but the update still trains the line along with the action. After training, the agent rarely commits while it has insufficient evidence and its belief line still names several answers. The policy learns from this reward using policy gradient or EM. It needs no judge, critic or reward model. 3 Experimental results. On three vision-language models and three benchmarks, RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average and by 10.4% with EM as the learner. It outperforms SFT and RL with the outcome reward in every setting. It also outperforms PPO with process reward from an LLM judge on average and uses 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours, or 4 times fewer with EM. Along with this gain, the share of answers given too early falls from 7687% to 4446%. Why the training helps. RLVB answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of episodes on the three benchmarks. The base model does so in 8%, 0.4% and 36% of episodes. Using belief line and the exact posterior, we find that the trained agent acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns with insufficient evidence at which its belief line still names several answers. The base model with the same line commits on 3 to 68% of those turns. When it commits, the trained agent gives the answer its line names, just like the base model. Across all turns, its belief line is not consistently more exact than the base models. The single answers it names are often wrong. Its steps add roughly as much evidence as the base models. In metacognitive terms, training mainly links decision control to the agents own monitoring. Monitoring improves only at the states that both agents reach, where the line names single answer too early less often. We expect better reading of the evidence to lead to better answers. Pro-Worlds Benchmark. We introduce Pro-Worlds, new benchmark of visual puzzles. The agent sees large world only through small window. It moves this window and must decide when it has seen enough to answer. Pro-Worlds tests this decision in visual worlds never seen in training.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: RL for language and vision-language agents. RL with outcome rewards has improved the reasoning of language models (Guo et al., 2025; Kimi Team, 2025; Shao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025). Self-training methods follow similar idea, as they sample the models own rationales and keep those that reach correct answer (Zelikman et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2024). For multi-turn agents, RAGEN (Wang et al., 2025b) finds that sparse and delayed rewards fail to reinforce the reasoning of each step. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) obtains finer credit by grouping the steps that share state. VAGEN (Wang et al., 2025a) adds turn-level reward for the agents estimate of the world state. These rewards still come from the outcome or from learned estimate, while RLVB computes its rewards from the exact posterior. Process rewards. Process reward models score each step of solution instead of only the final answer (Lightman et al., 2024). Most are trained on human or Monte Carlo labels, and their quality depends on how these labels are made (Zhang et al., 2025). Others learn from outcomes alone (Cui et al., 2026), reason before they judge (Khalifa et al., 2026), or derive the step reward from regularized RL objective (Yao et al., 2026). Closer to our setting, PRInTS (Lee et al., 2026) learns reward model for long-horizon information seeking. Our process reward is computed exactly by the environment, and it needs no reward model, no judge and no step labels. Belief states and information gathering. The belief state is the posterior over the hidden state. It is sufficient statistic for acting under partial observability (Åström, 1965; Kaelbling et al., 1998). The value of an evidence-gathering action is the information gained from it (Howard, 1966; Lindley, 1956). BEDLLM (Choudhury et al., 2026) asks the questions with the highest expected information gain at test time. Bayesian teaching (Qiu et al., 2026) fine-tunes model to imitate Bayesian assistant. CURIO (Wan et al., 2025) and ECHO (Nath et al., 2026) reward each turn in multi-turn interaction by how much it improves belief over hidden variable. Unlike these methods, RLVB uses lookahead on the exact posterior to value the decision to stop. It also compares several turns at the same history. Agent-BRACE (Singh et al., 2026) is closest to our work. It trains an agent in text environments to state its belief as claims about the environment, each with certainty word. Its policy acts on this belief instead of the history. An LLM judge grades these claims against the true hidden state rather than the posterior. When two answers are equally likely, the judge rewards claim that names only the true answer, just as an outcome reward rewards lucky guess. In RLVB, the agent is visual and states the set of answers it still sees as possible. The exact posterior scores its action and can also score this belief. As result, the reward is verifiable and needs no judge.

sections.title: 4.1 Benchmarks
sections.content: In all We evaluate on three benchmarks: HiddenGames, Pro-Worlds and RoboQuest (Liu et al., 2026). benchmarks, the answer is hidden. The agent must take actions to collect evidence and decide when it has seen enough to answer. It consists of seven tasks from existing agent benchmarks: MineSweeper (Wang et al., HiddenGames. 2026a), MiniGrid KeyCorridor (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2023), FrozenLake and Sokoban (Wang et al., 2025a), and three Tabletop tasks rendered in ManiSkill3 (Tao et al., 2025). We train on these tasks and test on 756 of their games with seeds, maps and colors never seen in training. Pro-Worlds. To assess transfer to out-of-domain visual tasks, we introduce Pro-Worlds, benchmark that tests how visual agents gather, retain and combine evidence before they commit to an answer. In each game, the agent sees larger world only through small window, moves the window to collect evidence, and must decide when it has seen enough to answer. The window shows one site of the world at time. The agent can make at most 35 moves before it names one of eight candidates (ten in Jigsaw) as its answer. We compute the exact posterior of every game from its game engine. teacher acting on this posterior solves every game in 14.7 moves on average. We test on 15 games (Face, Jigsaw, Kaleido, Bird, Fish, Recipe, Turtle, Balloon, Rocket, Bell, Bee, Candle, Sailboat, Barn and Lantern), with 20 plays of each. 8 RoboQuest. To test transfer to tasks without an exact posterior, we use the ten mobile manipulation tasks of RoboQuest (Liu et al., 2026). They take place in simulated kitchens and require search, inspection and interactive testing, such as finding the odd parcel by weighing. We test on 50 games of each task. The supplementary material gives further details of all three benchmarks.

sections.title: 4.2 Experiment Setup
sections.content: Models. We train three open-source vision-language models: Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking and Qwen3-VL-8BThinking (Bai et al., 2025), and Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026). Baselines. Base is the untrained model and outputs an action only. Base (w/ belief) is the same model with belief line before the action. We consider two groups of trained baselines. The first group acts without belief and learns from whole episodes. SFT fine-tunes the base model on the teachers actions in winning games. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) train on the outcome reward of each episode. PPO also learns critic. The second group learns from process reward. In PPO (belief + action), the model writes its belief as short claims with certainty words and then an action. PPO trains it with the outcome reward of the episode. learned value function carries this reward back to every turn. At each turn, an LLM judge (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026)) rewards the belief by checking its claims against the newest observation and the true hidden state. Only the belief gets per-turn reward. The decision to continue or to answer is rewarded only by the outcome of the episode. Both rewards of this baseline are based on the truth. The reward of RLVB is instead based on the evidence. The outcome reward pays correct answer even when it was guess. The judge rewards true claim even when the evidence does not support it. PPO (belief + action) also samples whole episodes and learns from one outcome per episode. RLVB instead samples multiple turns at each history and rewards each of them against the exact posterior. All methods train LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) for up to 50 updates on the same tasks. At every turn, every method receives the full history of its actions and observations but not its earlier reasoning. Metrics. We test the adapter after the last update of each run. Each test runs three times with different sampling seeds. We report the mean accuracy over the three runs1. Accuracy is the share of episodes ending with the correct answer. The supplementary material lists the settings of RLVB.

sections.title: 4.6 Why RLVB works
sections.content: Summary. RLVB gains because it answers with more evidence. It gets this evidence by acting on its own belief line. When the evidence is insufficient and its belief line still names several answers, RLVB commits at 0.1 to 2.2% of turns, against 3 to 68% for Base (w/ belief). As result, its answers come mostly after its belief line names single answer (RQ3). The belief line itself is not consistently more accurate. Over all turns, compared to Base (w/ belief), it is exact more often in some settings and less often in others, and the single answers it names are often wrong (RQ1). RLVBs steps add about as much evidence as the base models steps (RQ2). There are three possible explanations for RLVBs gain. The trained agent could read its evidence better (RQ1), take steps that bring more evidence (RQ2), or act on what its belief line says (RQ3). In terms of metacognition, RQ1 and RQ2 look at monitoring the evidence. RQ3 looks at whether controlling the decision follows this monitoring. At every turn, the exact posterior measures how strongly the evidence gathered so far settles the answer. This lets us test each explanation. We call each evidence-gathering action step. We call the evidence sufficient when the exact posterior of the top answer is at least 0.95. RoboQuest has no posterior, so there the evidence is sufficient once all evidence requirements of the task are met. We define the evidence at the answer as the top answers posterior on the turn when the agent commits. On RoboQuest, it is the share of requirements met on that turn. belief line is exact when it names exactly the answers that are still possible. Base is the base model without belief line. Base (w/ belief) is the same model with belief line. In this section, HiddenGames means its five tasks with an answer, and RoboQuest means its eight tasks with countable requirements. The accuracies therefore differ from those in table 1. Section gives details of these measures and further tests. The evidence at the answer. Figure 5 groups each methods episodes by the evidence at the answer. HiddenGames and Pro-Worlds use four levels because the posterior takes only few values there. RoboQuest uses six levels. It answers with sufficient evidence in 51% of HiddenGames episodes, 12% on Pro-Worlds and 74% on RoboQuest, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for Base and 20%, 3% and 57% for PPO (belief + action). sections.title: 5 Limitations
sections.content: RLVB needs task with known rules. The environment can compute the exact posterior only when it knows the prior over the hidden answer and the likelihood of each observation. Many puzzles, games, and simulated 22 household tasks meet this condition. For tasks with unknown or open-ended rules, the posterior must be estimated. Very large action spaces need shallower or sampled lookahead. The cost of the teachers lookahead grows with the number of actions and observations. Finally, belief line names set of possible answers. This set states the posterior exactly only when every possible answer is equally likely. The belief line cannot express finer degrees of certainty. With training, wrong answers given with enough evidence also rise from 24% to 1015% of the episodes, mostly in the Tabletop tasks (tables 6 and 30). On these tasks, the agent misreads observations that already settle the answer. It then gives the wrong answer that its belief line names (section 4.6). The action term also scores which step the agent takes, but the trained agent does not choose more informative steps. On Pro-Worlds, step by the posterior teacher raises the posterior by 5.9%, compared to 0.7 to 1.3% for step by any method. The trained agents also stay far below the posterior teacher (for example 32.4% against 100% on Pro-Worlds). The agents have not yet learned much of what the exact posterior allows.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We showed that simulator can compute the exact posterior of an evidence-seeking task from its privileged information. This posterior gives process reward at every turn. The posterior scores the agents choice between taking more steps and answering. It can also score the agents stated belief. RLVB learns from this reward with policy gradient, and RLVB (EM) learns from it with EM. Across three vision-language models and three benchmarks, both RLVB learners improve the base model in every setting. With the same learner, the posterior process reward beats the outcome reward by 18.1% on average. On each of the three benchmarks, RLVB also beats process reward from an LLM judge on average. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12%, and 74% of episodes, compared to 8%, 0.4%, and 36% for the base model. It does this by acting on its own belief. With the same belief line, it commits on only 0.1 to 2.2% of turns with insufficient evidence where this line still names several answers, compared to 3 to 68% for the base model. Across all turns, its belief line is not consistently more exact than the base models. Each of its steps adds about as much evidence as step from the base model. check in the harness does not raise the base models accuracy on HiddenGames and Pro-Worlds because the harness cannot read the observations. We expect better reading of the evidence to carry into the answers when an agent acts on its belief. RLVBs steps are not yet more informative than the base models. An agent with sufficient evidence can still misread its observations. We want to extend RLVB to tasks where the posterior must be learned, to improve the choice of the next step, and to train the agent to read its observations correctly once its evidence is sufficient.

sections.title: E Benchmarks in detail
sections.content: HiddenGames. HiddenGames is mixture of seven tasks from different agent benchmarks. In each task, the agent must find hidden target from what it observes. MineSweeper (Wang et al., 2026a) hides the mines of small board. In MiniGrid KeyCorridor (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2023), the agent must find the room that holds the key. In FrozenLake (Wang et al., 2025a), we hide the goal and the distant holes. In Sokoban (Wang et al., 2025a), we hide the target square. The agent must thus explore before it can plan. The three Tabletop tasks are rendered scenes of table (Tao et al., 2025). The agent must find which button lights which lamp, which cup hides named object as in figure 1, or which block slides farther. It sees only two camera images after each action. The environment of every task knows the prior and the likelihood of each observation. The teacher of section 3.2 can thus compute the exact posterior. We train and test on all seven tasks. The test split consists of 756 games whose seeds, maps and Tabletop colors are never seen in training. Pro-Worlds. We introduce Pro-Worlds, benchmark of how visual agents gather, retain and combine evidence before they commit to an answer. Each game hides one of few answers, for example which emotion face shows or which fish picture shows. The game draws its world as grid of sites, each tile of 16 16 color cells. The agent sees one site at time through window, rendered as 256 256 picture. At each turn, the agent either moves the window by one site with ACTION: MOVE UP, DOWN, LEFT or RIGHT, or submits an answer with ACTION: SUBMIT. move at the edge keeps the window in place but still counts. play allows at most 35 moves. It ends with submission, with move when no moves are left, or after 43 turns. The prompt gives the rules of the game, the list of answers and every picture seen so far with its position. We place the start where the first view never decides the answer. The engine knows every possible world of game and can thus compute the exact posterior. This posterior holds the worlds consistent with every site seen so far, with the same prior weight for each answer. As in the other benchmarks, submission is premature when the posterior of the top answer is below 0.95. Table 14 lists the 15 test games. We test on 20 plays of each game, 300 plays in all. Eight of the games are the training games of the benchmark, drawn at random from the 15. However, no model in this paper trains on Pro-Worlds. RoboQuest. RoboQuest (Liu et al., 2026) consists of ten mobile manipulation tasks built around search, inspection and interactive testing. In each task, such as finding the odd parcel by weighing, the agent must gather information through physical interaction before it decides to finish. Liu et al. report that agents often stop exploring too early (Liu et al., 2026). Unlike the other two benchmarks, RoboQuest runs in physics simulator of real kitchens. Its possible states cannot be listed, and there is no exact posterior. Many of its answers are also actions in the scene rather than choice among listed options. The belief lines of all agents are therefore free text, such as Possible: blue water bottle may be in drawer 2 or another compartment. We use RoboQuest to test whether what an agent learns from exact posteriors transfers to task without one. We use the text version of its decision-level setting, where the agent chooses high-level actions and scripted helpers carry them out. We test on 50 games of each task, 500 games in all.

Because 51 on-policy sampling is the more common choice, we also train an on-policy variant of RLVB on Qwen3-VL-4B. The only difference is that this variant samples small set of new games before every update. Figure 13 compares the two approaches. Figure 13 Sampling in phases against on-policy sampling (Qwen3-VL-4B). Left: training time, where the two jumps for RLVB come from its two sampling passes. Middle: the number of turns in the games sampled for training, with the thin line showing each update and the thick line showing the mean of five updates. Right: accuracy on the three benchmarks. The first difference is cost: RLVB takes 6.4 hours in total, with its two sampling passes taking 47 and 74 minutes and each of its 50 updates then taking about 5 minutes. We stopped the on-policy variant after 46 updates, which took 20.8 hours. Because every update of the variant includes sampling, updates grow slower as training proceeds, averaging 20 minutes over the first ten updates and 39 minutes over the last ten. As the middle panel of figure 13 shows, the games sampled by the on-policy variant lengthen from about 5 turns in the first ten updates to about 20 in the last ten because the model answers less and less often. Its extra steps in MiniGrid and MineSweeper bring almost no evidence  (table 37)  . likely reason is the reward. It gives very low value to an early answer, and it charges very little for one more step after the evidence is sufficient. Under on-policy sampling, each update draws its games from model that already answers slightly less often than the previous one. The middle panel of figure 13 is consistent with this drift toward fewer answers. With phases, in contrast, the model playing the games is renewed only once during training. The on-policy variants reasoning is also cut off more often at the 8,192-token limit. After cutoff, the variant mostly takes more steps instead of answering. We keep the phases because they take third of the time and produce model that ends fewer episodes without an answer.
